Differential equation

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Analysis
OurBigBook.com Words: 34k Articles: 440
A differential equation is an equation relating an unknown function to its derivatives. It specifies how change depends on the present state, and sometimes on the independent variables themselves. A solution of a differential equation is a function satisfying that relation throughout a stated domain; giving a formula without its domain can conceal a point where the equation is undefined.
The central idea is to turn a local law into a whole trajectory. For example, y′=ry, with constant r, says that the instantaneous derivative is proportional to the current value. If y(0)=100 and r=0.2 per day, the solution of a differential equation is y(t)=100e0.2t, so y(5)=100e≈271.83. This is an ideal growth model assuming a constant proportional rate; the exponential function emerges from repeatedly applying the same local rule. Changing the sign of r gives exponential decay.
An ordinary differential equation uses one independent variable. A partial differential equation can involve several, such as space and time, and uses partial derivatives. Additional information selects a particular solution of a differential equation: an initial condition describes a starting state, whereas a boundary condition imposes constraints at the edge of a domain. The useful questions extend beyond finding a formula: does a solution of a differential equation exist, is it unique, and what happens to it over time?

Orthogonal trajectory

Words: 84
Differential equation OurBigBook.com
An orthogonal trajectory intersects every regular member of a specified family of plane curves at a right angle. If eliminating the family parameter gives its tangent slope dy/dx=F(x,y), the dot product of the two tangent directions gives the orthogonal slope dy/dx=−1/F(x,y) wherever both slopes are finite and nonzero. Vertical and horizontal tangent directions are interpreted geometrically. For the family y=cxn with n>0, eliminating c gives F=ny/x, and the orthogonal trajectories satisfy x2+ny2=C. For n=2 these are ellipses; for n=1 they are circles.

Stationary solution (∂t​u=0)

Words: 52
Differential equation OurBigBook.com
A stationary solution of an evolution differential equation is independent of time. Substituting ∂t​u=0 leaves the spatial boundary value problem that determines its profile. For an ordinary differential equation this is an equilibrium; for a partial differential equation it may vary in space. A stationary profile need not have zero flux, although zero flux is forced in a one-dimensional conserved system with reflecting endpoints.

Direction field (y′=f(t,y))

Words: 183
Differential equation OurBigBook.com
A direction field for y′=f(t,y) places a short segment with slope f(t,y) at each sampled point where f is defined. A function graph of a solution of a differential equation follows these segments: its tangent line has exactly the prescribed slope. Segment length is a drawing choice, rather than a speed; arrows, if used, point toward increasing t. An isocline collects points with one common slope.
For Newton's law of cooling, y′=−0.1(y−20) with time in minutes and temperature in degrees Celsius, the slopes at y=80,40,20,10 are respectively −6,−2,0,1 degrees Celsius per minute. Each horizontal row is an isocline, because this autonomous differential equation has no explicit time dependence. Above 20 the solutions of a differential equation descend, below 20 they rise, and y=20 is an equilibrium point.
The highlighted initial condition y(0)=80 selects one curve from the family. The picture reveals approach to the equilibrium point before any algebra is done. Under the hypotheses of the Picard-Lindelöf theorem, distinct function graphs of solutions cannot cross or even meet in the time-state plane. A direction field alone does not guarantee uniqueness: several curves can share a tangent line at the same point when those hypotheses fail. See the delayed-start example under initial value problem.
This geometric interpretation is developed in Direction Fields, Isoclines, Integral Curves.

Differential equation OurBigBook.com

{(x,y)∈D:f(x,y)=k}.
(1)
Here k is a constant. At every point of this isocline, the direction field prescribes a tangent vector proportional to (1,k) for a solution of a differential equation. It does not generally prescribe the tangent line of the isocline itself. The level set can have several components or fail to be a smooth curve, and points outside D are excluded.
For example, take y′=x−y on the whole plane. Its isoclines are the parallel straight lines
x−y=k,y=x−k.
(2)
Each line has slope 1, while the direction field along it has slope k. Thus the isocline y=x carries horizontal segments even though the line itself rises. A function graph of a solution of a differential equation follows the segments, rather than following this line. Only the isocline with k=1, namely y=x−1, is also a solution of a differential equation.[ref]
The first-order linear differential equation has the exact family

For A=0 the solution of a differential equation stays on the k=1 isocline; for other A it moves through different isoclines. These formulas check the pictured trajectories by direct differentiation, independently of how the direction field was sampled.
The zero-slope isocline f(x,y)=0 is called a nullcline. Below the nullcline y=x in this example, y′>0; above it, y′<0. For A>0, the solution of a differential equation meets it at x=logA, where y′=0 and y′′=1, a strict local minimum. The nullcline is therefore a useful guide to turning points, although it is not itself a solution of a differential equation. In the equivalent planar autonomous differential equation x˙=1, y˙​=x−y, it is the nullcline for the second component; there is no equilibrium point, because the first component never vanishes.
This makes isoclines useful even when no explicit solution of a differential equation is available: organize a direction field by common slopes, read where function graphs rise or fall, and identify possible turning points on nullclines.

An autonomous differential equation has f independent of t; its equilibrium points satisfy f(y∗​)=0 and give constant solutions of a differential equation. Equations with explicit time dependence can instead respond to a changing environment.

More generally, set w=f/g and solve the holomorphic linear system f′=bf+cg, g′=−af. Its quotient satisfies w′=aw2+bw+c directly. At a zero of g with a=0, uniqueness prevents f=0 there, so g′=−af=0 and the pole is simple. Any cluster value where the vector field is holomorphic permits uniform local continuation by the Picard-Lindelöf theorem. Otherwise the cluster set lies in finitely many coefficient poles, so it is a singleton. At a pole of the vector field, the inverse equation is holomorphic; its solution has a finite-order critical point, giving a convergent root expansion. The reciprocal dependent variable handles infinity. Points where both reduced numerator and denominator vanish belong to the fixed exceptional set and are excluded from this argument.

Nonlinear ordinary differential equations can describe state-dependent growth such as the logistic differential equation, whose negative quadratic term limits growth instead of accelerating it without bound. Recognizing the distinction tells us when we may assemble solutions of a differential equation from simpler pieces and when we must account for their interaction. See MIT's worked counterexample to nonlinear superposition.

This nonlinear ordinary differential equation governs the amplitude of a complex oscillator solution. Independent real solutions of y′′+p(x)y=0 can be combined into a nonvanishing complex solution; its modulus satisfies the equation with c equal to the squared Wronskian. A real positive amplitude and a conserved phase flux give an exact representation, not merely a WKB approximation.

Logistic differential equation (N′=rN(1−N/K))

Words: 928 Articles: 1
Nonlinear ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
The logistic differential equation is the nonlinear ordinary differential equation
dtdN​=rN(1−KN​),r>0,K>0,N(0)=N0​≥0.
(39)
As a mathematical model of population dynamics, it treats abundance N as a continuous nonnegative quantity. The constant r has units of inverse time, while the carrying capacity K has the same units as N. The useful idea is to combine growth resembling exponential growth at low abundance with a slowing approach to a finite abundance. The three trajectories below already show an important distinction: starting above the carrying capacity gives a decreasing curve, whereas starting below it gives an increasing one.
For N>0, dividing the derivative by abundance gives the instantaneous per-capita rate:
NN′​=r(1−KN​).
(40)
It decreases linearly with N: it approaches r at low abundance, is r/2 at N=K/2, vanishes at the carrying capacity, and is negative above it. This per-capita rate differs from the total rate N′, which also counts how many individuals contribute. It is an instantaneous rate, rather than a fixed percentage increase over a whole day. The linear per-capita assumption and the resulting qualitative picture are developed in MIT 18.03SC's logistic-model notes.
Writing f(N)=rN(1−N/K), the equilibrium points satisfy f(N)=0, so the constant solutions of a differential equation are N(t)=0 and N(t)=K. The phase line points upward for 0<N<K and downward for N>K. Also f′(0)=r>0 and f′(K)=−r<0: the criterion for fixed point stability for an autonomous differential equation makes zero an unstable equilibrium and K an asymptotically stable equilibrium point. Every positive initial condition approaches K as t→∞; N0​=0 stays exactly zero. Instability of zero means that a small positive population grows away from it, not that a zero population spontaneously appears.
For every N0​>0, the unique solution of a differential equation for all t≥0 is
N(t)=1+(N0​K​−1)e−rtK​.
(41)
The denominator is positive on this domain, including when N0​>K. For 0<N0​<K, this is a translated and scaled logistic function; its extension to all real times is a sigmoid function. For N0​>K the coefficient of the exponential function is negative, and the future curve instead decreases toward K. No nonconstant positive solution of a differential equation crosses K or reaches it at finite time. A short derivation uses the dimensionless variable z=K/N−1: the chain rule gives z′=−rz, so exponential decay yields z(t)=(K/N0​−1)e−rt. The substitution divides by N, so the zero equilibrium point must be included separately.
The total growth rate is a downward-opening quadratic function of abundance. Completing the square gives its maximum without solving the differential equation:
f(N)=4rK​−Kr​(N−2K​)2,maxN≥0​f(N)=4rK​at N=2K​.
(42)
The balance is beautiful: more individuals contribute to growth, but each contributes less, and the strongest total increase occurs halfway to the carrying capacity. This is a maximum over possible abundances. A trajectory starting above K/2 never passes through that abundance in its future.
The chain rule connects this maximum to the shape of the time trajectory through its second derivative:
N′′=f′(N)N′=r(1−K2N​)N′.
(43)
For 0<N0​<K/2, the trajectory initially has convexity and then concavity, with its one future inflection point at
t1/2​=r1​ln(N0​K​−1),N(t1/2​)=2K​.
(44)
For N0​=K/2, this point lies at the initial time, with concavity for t>0. For K/2<N0​<K, the inflection point belongs to the past extension, so the future trajectory has concavity throughout. Above K, the decreasing trajectory has convexity and no inflection point. The two constant solutions of a differential equation have no change of concavity. Thus an entire logistic function has an S shape, but its observed future segment need not show both bends. See also [ref].
For the plotted example with K=1000, r=0.4day−1 and N0​=100, time t measured in days gives
N(t)=1+9e−0.4t1000​,N(5)≈450.85306,N(10)≈858.48645.
(45)
The initial total rate is N′(0)=0.4⋅100⋅0.9=36 individuals per day, and the initial per-capita rate is 0.36day−1. The fastest total increase is rK/4=100 individuals per day, reached at t1/2​=ln9/0.4≈5.49306 days. At that time the per-capita rate has already fallen to 0.2day−1.
These parameters are illustrative choices, rather than an empirical fit. The equation specifies deterministic evolution under a phenomenological assumption: it summarizes how net growth depends on abundance without separately modelling every process that affects it. The carrying capacity is a parameter for a specified setting, not a universal constant for all populations. In his 1838 paper "Notice sur la loi que la population suit dans son accroissement", Correspondance mathématique et physique 10, pp. 113–121, Pierre-François Verhulst proposed p′=mp−np2, equivalent to this equation with r=m and K=m/n. He also noted that different assumed growth-retarding terms could describe the observations similarly while giving very different limiting populations. This is an early illustration of why a good-looking curve alone does not establish a unique long-term prediction.[ref]
The logistic differential equation describes continuous time. The logistic map instead advances in discrete steps and can exhibit a period-doubling cascade and Devaney chaos; the monotone positive trajectories here cannot. Their connection through the forward Euler method is explained under Euler discretization of logistic growth, where a large step can introduce behaviour absent from the original differential equation.
Euler discretization of logistic growth (λ=1+rΔt)
Words: 61
Logistic differential equation OurBigBook.com
The forward Euler method applied to the logistic differential equation y′=ry(1−ay) becomes the logistic map after u=a(λ−1)y/λ, λ=1+rΔt. The positive equilibrium point of the differential equation has perturbations decaying as e−rt. Its discrete fixed-point multiplier is 1−rΔt=2−λ: for rΔt>2, the discretization has an artificial oscillatory instability, leading initially to alternation on successive steps. This contrasts with the positive perturbation multiplier e−rΔt of the exact time-step map.

Picard-Lindelöf theorem (y′=f(t,y),y(t0​)=y0​)

Words: 2k Articles: 11
Ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
Let U⊂R×Rd be an open set and f:U→Rd a continuous function. Suppose f is locally Lipschitz in the state y, with a Lipschitz constant uniform on a sufficiently small time-state neighborhood of each point. Then each (t0​,y0​)∈U determines a unique local solution of a differential equation to the displayed initial value problem, on an interval around t0​. This is the local theorem in Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems by Gerald Teschl.
For example, y′=y, y(0)=1, has the solution of a differential equation y(t)=et: its derivative is itself and its starting value is 1. The Lipschitz constant is L=1, since ∣u−v∣=∣f(t,u)−f(t,v)∣. Thus uniqueness follows even before computing y(1)=e≈2.71828183. Picard iteration below constructs this exponential function one polynomial at a time.
The Lipschitz condition has real content. For the continuous function involving a square root,
f(y)=2max(y,0)​,y′=f(y),y(0)=0,
(46)
each waiting time c≥0 gives a different forward solution of a differential equation:
yc​(t)={0,(t−c)2,​0≤t≤c,t>c.​
(47)
The constant solution of a differential equation y(t)=0 is another choice. At t=2, delays c=0,1,2 give y=4,1,0 respectively. Before the join, both sides of the ordinary differential equation are zero; afterwards, yc′​=2(t−c)=2yc​​. Both one-sided derivatives at c are zero, so the join is valid. All these trajectories can also be extended by zero to t<0. The failed Lipschitz condition is visible in the quotient
∣ε−0∣∣f(ε)−f(0)∣​=ε​2​⟶∞(ε↓0).
(48)
For ε=10−2,10−4,10−6 this quotient is 20,200,2000. Continuity still allows local existence by the Peano existence theorem; it cannot choose a waiting time. MIT's 18.034 Lecture 2, Example 2.3 develops the same waiting-time mechanism for a different ordinary differential equation, y′=3y2/3.
The useful promise is that an initial condition and a sufficiently regular local rule select one trajectory. It justifies comparing models and following trajectories without an arbitrary choice at each instant. A locally Lipschitz continuous rule need not keep that trajectory bounded: y′=1+y2 meets the theorem's hypotheses everywhere but has finite-time blowup. Longer existence is governed by the finite-dimensional continuation criterion.

On a smaller interval of radius η, the displayed Picard operator maps continuous curves in that closed ball into itself when ηM≤k, and it is a contraction mapping in the supremum norm when ηLf​<1. Picard iteration (yn+1​=Pyn​)

Words: 803 Articles: 4
Picard-Lindelöf theorem OurBigBook.com
Picard iteration replaces a tentative trajectory by the accumulated integral of its proposed rate. For an initial value problem y′=f(t,y), y(t0​)=y0​, define the Picard map and its starting function by
(Pu)(t)=y0​+∫t0​t​f(s,u(s))ds,y0​(t)≡y0​,yn+1​=Pyn​.
(51)
Here y0​(t) is the constant starting trajectory; the same symbol without its argument denotes the initial state. A fixed point of P solves this integral equation, and the fundamental theorem of calculus gives the original ordinary differential equation.
For y′=y, y(0)=1, successive integrals give
y0​(t)y1​(t)y2​(t)y3​(t)y4​(t)yn​(t)​=1,=1+t,=1+t+2t2​,=1+t+2t2​+6t3​,=1+t+2t2​+6t3​+24t4​,=k=0∑n​k!tk​.​
(52)
At t=1, the first five values are 1,2,2.5,2.66666667,2.70833333, while e≈2.71828183. The fourth polynomial misses by about 0.00994850. On 0≤t≤1, every omitted term of the exponential series is nonnegative and increasing, so the largest error occurs at t=1. The tail tends to zero, giving uniform convergence to the exponential function on this interval.
The beauty of Picard iteration is that each proposed trajectory supplies a better rate history for the next one. For this example, one integration adds exactly the next term of the exponential series. In general, the integrals may be difficult to compute, but the construction still explains local existence and uniqueness.
The short contraction mapping argument needs two independent controls. Choose a time-state cylinder [t0​−a,t0​+a]×Br​(y0​)⊂U on which
∥f(t,z)∥≤M,∥f(t,u)−f(t,v)∥≤L∥u−v∥.
(53)
The second bound is the uniform local Lipschitz condition. Set J=[t0​−h,t0​+h] with 0<h≤a, Mh≤r and Lh<1. In the function space of continuous functions J→Rd, use the supremum norm ∥u∥∞​=supt∈J​∥u(t)∥. On its closed ball ∥u−y0​∥∞​≤r, direct integral estimates give
∥Pu−y0​∥∞​≤Mh≤r,∥Pu−Pv∥∞​≤Lh∥u−v∥∞​.
(54)
Thus the map preserves the closed ball and is a contraction mapping there. This closed ball is a complete metric space, so the contraction mapping theorem gives convergence to exactly one fixed point. Any other local solution of a differential equation stays in the same ball after shortening its interval, and hence agrees there.
For y′=y, take r=1, so ∣y∣≤2 in the state ball and M=2, L=1. Choosing h=1/2 gives Mh=1 and Lh=1/2, with the actual solution satisfying ∣e1/2−1∣≈0.64872127<1. The plotted interval [0,1] is longer than this simple guarantee: the explicitly computed exponential series converges there anyway. The condition Lh<1 is sufficient for this one-step contraction mapping argument, rather than a necessary lifespan bound.

Finite-dimensional continuation criterion (T+​<∞ ⟹ escape from every compact subset of U)

Words: 455
Picard-Lindelöf theorem OurBigBook.com
Under the Picard-Lindelöf theorem's hypotheses on U⊂R×Rd, extend a solution of a differential equation as far as possible, to a maximal interval (T−​,T+​). If T+​<∞, the time-state trajectory (t,y(t)) must eventually leave every compact subset of U. Equivalently, confinement near T+​ to one compact subset of U permits continuation past T+​. See Teschl, Section 2.6, Lemma 2.14 and Corollaries 2.15–2.16, pp. 52–53.
The domain restriction matters even for a bounded trajectory. Restrict y′=1, y(0)=0, to U=R×(−1,1). Then y(t)=t exists in this domain only for −1<t<1; at t=1/2,3/4,9/10 its values are 1/2,3/4,9/10. As t↑1, it approaches the excluded boundary point (1,1) while remaining bounded. Its trajectory cannot fit into any compact subset of U near that endpoint. This is escape from a finite domain, without finite-time blowup in norm. Enlarging the domain to R×R gives the same formula y(t)=t for every real t.
Conversely, y′=y, y(0)=1, stays in the compact set [0,T]×[1,eT] for every fixed T>0. Its growing exponential function is unbounded over the entire future, but has no finite-time blowup. At T=2, its largest value on [0,2] is only e2≈7.38905610. The relevant question is boundedness before each finite endpoint, rather than one bound valid forever. The tangent function in the diagram under the Picard-Lindelöf theorem illustrates the other possibility: its norm escapes every bound before T=π/2.
This criterion is useful because an estimate can secure continuation without an explicit formula. In a finite-dimensional vector space, a bounded closed ball is compact; a bounded state trajectory therefore supplies the needed compact set when its time-state closure is inside the domain. That final proviso prevents mistaking a domain boundary for finite-time blowup.
A common sufficient estimate comes from global Lipschitz continuity in the state. Assume U=I×Rd for an open time interval I, with f continuous and a Lipschitz constant L≥0 valid for all states on each compact time interval under consideration. For [t0​,T]⊂I, let B=supt0​≤s≤T​∥f(s,0)∥, finite by continuity. Then ∥f(t,y)∥≤B+L∥y∥, and the Gronwall inequality gives, for t0​≤t≤T wherever the solution already exists,
∥y(t)∥≤⎩⎨⎧​∥y0​∥eL(t−t0​)+LB​(eL(t−t0​)−1),∥y0​∥+B(t−t0​),​L>0,L=0.​
(58)
For instance, y′=y+1, y(0)=0, has L=B=1 and the exact solution y(t)=et−1, attaining this estimate; at t=1 the value is e−1≈1.71828183. Finite bounds of this kind give continuation throughout I, with the analogous estimate backwards in time. When I=R, this gives existence for all real times. If I has a finite endpoint, it gives no continuation beyond that prescribed domain. The underlying linear-growth criterion is [ref].
A brief explanation of the continuation mechanism suffices: within the protecting compact set, the continuous function f is bounded, say by M. The integral equation yields ∥y(t)−y(s)∥≤M∣t−s∣ near the finite endpoint, so y(t) has a limit y∗​. The protecting compact set puts (T+​,y∗​) inside U. Restarting the initial value problem there and using local uniqueness joins the trajectories.

Finite-time blowup (limt↑T​∥y(t)∥=∞,T<∞)

Ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A solution of a differential equation has finite-time blowup in norm when ∥y(t)∥→∞ as t approaches a finite endpoint T of its maximal interval of existence. This is stronger than merely approaching an excluded boundary of an open state domain while staying bounded. The finite-dimensional continuation criterion distinguishes these obstructions; for a locally Lipschitz continuous ordinary differential equation on I×Rd, a finite maximal endpoint inside I necessarily entails finite-time blowup.
A simple example with a smooth right-hand side is
y′=1+y2,y(0)=0,y(t)=tant,−2π​<t<2π​.
(59)
The derivative identity (tant)′=1+tan2t verifies the equation and the initial condition. Also ∣u2−v2∣=∣u−v∣∣u+v∣≤2R∣u−v∣ for ∣u∣,∣v∣≤R, giving local Lipschitz continuity and therefore uniqueness. Yet the positive blowup time is T=π/2≈1.57079633. Computed values show the accelerating growth:
y(1)≈1.55740772,y(1.4)≈5.79788372,y(1.5)≈14.10141995.
(60)
The right panel under the Picard-Lindelöf theorem deliberately clips its vertical axis at 10: the trajectory has already left the picture at t=arctan10≈1.47112767, before reaching T. A plot ceiling is a display limit, not a finite value at blowup.
The tangent function also quantifies the last part of the trajectory. With δ=T−t>0,
y(T−δ)=sinδcosδ​,δy(T−δ)⟶1(δ↓0).
(61)
Thus the height is approximately the reciprocal of the remaining time. At remaining times δ=0.1,0.01,0.001, the heights are approximately 9.96664442,99.99666664,999.99966667. These follow from the sine and cosine limits at zero and explain the steep rise without relying on the appearance of a clipped function graph.
The distinction is useful when interpreting a solution of a differential equation: uniqueness certifies a trajectory while it exists, while growth estimates decide how far it can be followed. For y′=1+y2, the Lipschitz constant 2R on a bounded state interval grows with R, and the right-hand side grows quadratically. There is no global Lipschitz constant or linear-growth bound of the kind used by the finite-dimensional continuation criterion. Smoothness at every finite state is entirely compatible with finite-time blowup.

Linear differential equation (L[y]=g(t))

Words: 3k Articles: 19
Ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A scalar linear differential equation of order n≥1 has the form
L[y](t)=an​(t)y(n)(t)+an−1​(t)y(n−1)(t)+⋯+a1​(t)y′(t)+a0​(t)y(t)=g(t).
(62)
Here the coefficients aj​ and the forcing term g are prescribed functions of the independent variable t. A classical solution of a differential equation is an n-times differentiable function satisfying the identity at every point of its interval. The unknown function y and its derivatives enter to the first power, without products between them or coefficients depending on y. Equivalently, the differential operator L is a linear map: for constant scalars α,β,
L[αu+βv]=αL[u]+βL[v].
(63)
The forcing term may be zero, giving a homogeneous linear differential equation, or nonzero, giving an inhomogeneous linear differential equation. Linearity of L does not mean that every function graph of a solution of a differential equation is a straight line.
To use the usual order-n initial value problem theory on an interval I, assume that an​(t)=0 throughout I and that all aj​ and g are continuous functions there. Dividing by an​ normalizes the highest derivative; specifying y(t0​),y′(t0​),…,y(n−1)(t0​) at t0​∈I then selects one solution of a differential equation throughout I. A zero of an​ needs separate analysis: one cannot divide through it and retain these conclusions. The first-order normalization appears in OpenStax's definition and standard form of linear equations; the corresponding system theorem is in MIT's existence and uniqueness notes for linear systems.
The coefficients need not be linear functions of t. For example, t2y′+y=0 is a linear differential equation on t>0, although t2 is quadratic. Its solution of a differential equation with initial condition y(1)=1 is y(t)=e1/t−1: its derivative is y′=−y/t2, so substitution gives t2y′+y=0, and y(2)=e−1/2≈0.60653. The zero of the highest coefficient at t=0 explains the domain restriction. In contrast, y′+y2=0, yy′+y=0 and y′+siny=0 are nonlinear ordinary differential equations because of their dependence on the unknown function. Variable coefficients and nonlinear ordinary differential equations are different issues; see MIT's definitions and examples of first-order linear equations.
The practical benefit of linearity is that it separates the effect of the initial condition from the effect of the forcing term. Once one particular solution yp​ satisfies L[yp​]=g, every solution of a differential equation is
y=yp​+h,h∈kerL.
(64)
Here kerL is the kernel of a linear map, consisting of solutions of a differential equation to the associated homogeneous linear differential equation. Indeed, L[y−yp​]=g−g=0, and conversely L[yp​+h]=g+0=g. Thus the family for a fixed forcing term is an affine space obtained by translating kerL. If g is not identically zero, the zero function is absent, so this family is not a vector space under the usual operations on functions. This short argument explains why a general solution is a particular solution plus a homogeneous solution.

For a continuous periodic coefficient matrix A(t+L)=A(t), a fundamental matrix X for X′=A(t)X, normalized by X(0)=I, obeys X(t+L)=X(t)X(L). The invertible matrix X(L) has a complex matrix logarithm; set B=L−1logX(L) and P(t)=X(t)e−tB. Since X(L)=eLB commutes with B, direct substitution gives P(t+L)=P(t) and proves the factorization. A real logarithm is not required for this complex representation.
The eigenvalues of X(L) are Floquet multipliers. All solutions are bounded for forward time when every multiplier has modulus at most one and those on the unit circle have no nontrivial Jordan blocks. In a real undamped second-order scalar equation with no first-derivative term, the monodromy determinant is one. Distinct conjugate unit-modulus multipliers give bounded solutions; a nontrivial Jordan block at multiplier 1 or −1 gives an unbounded second solution even when one periodic or antiperiodic solution exists.

The instantaneous logarithmic derivative keeps oscillating even though its average over complete periods is exactly a. Sampling at the same phase in each period removes the modulation altogether: y(nT)=mny(0).
For the general finite-dimensional homogeneous linear differential equation x′=A(t)x, assume that A is continuous on the real line and T-periodic, with T>0. Normalize its fundamental matrix by Φ(0)=I and set M=Φ(T). The maximal asymptotic exponential rate, using any induced matrix norm, is
γ=limt→∞​tlog∥Φ(t)∥​=Tlogρ(M)​,ρ(M)=maxj​∣mj​∣.

Here ρ(M) is the spectral radius, mj​ are the Floquet multipliers, and invertibility gives ρ(M)>0. This concerns growth of the solution operator; it does not say that every initial condition attains the maximum.[ref]
To prove the formula, write t=nT+s with 0≤s<T. Periodicity and uniqueness give

For a particular nonzero initial condition v, decompose v into the generalized eigenspaces of M over the complex numbers. The rate of Φ(t)v is the largest T−1log∣mj​∣ among components that are nonzero. Generic data have a component in the dominant generalized eigenspaces and attain γ; data contained in the sum of the subdominant generalized eigenspaces have a smaller rate. For example, with A=diag(0.2,−0.3), the maximal rate is 0.2, while v=(0,1) decays at rate −0.3. These invariant subspaces describe initial data at phase zero. Their transported versions E(t)=Φ(t)E(0) can vary with time and satisfy E(t+T)=E(t).
A negative Floquet growth rate allows temporary amplification. For the constant non-normal matrix
A=(−10​10−1​),etA=e−t(10​10t1​),
(71)
the initial condition v=(0,1) has Euclidean norm e−t100t2+1​, which rises from 1 to about 3.697 at t=1 before eventually decaying. Its exponential rate is still −1: the Jordan block contributes a polynomial factor, whose logarithm divided by t tends to zero. At a unit-modulus Floquet multiplier, such polynomial growth can even be unbounded with zero exponential rate; A=(00​10​) gives etAv=(t,1). Thus zero Floquet growth rate alone proves neither boundedness nor a periodic solution.

Floquet theory OurBigBook.com
For the homogeneous linear differential equation Y˙=K(t)Y with continuous coefficient matrix of period P>0, the monodromy matrix of a periodic linear system is the one-period map from Y(0) to Y(P). If X is any fundamental matrix,
N=X(P)X(0)−1,Y(P)=NY(0).
(72)
Its eigenvalues are the Floquet multipliers. Multipliers are nonzero, since a fundamental matrix is invertible. Changing the starting phase conjugates N, so the Floquet multipliers and Jordan blocks are independent of that choice.[ref]
This turns a continuous-time problem into repeated matrix multiplication:
Y(nP)=NnY(0).
(73)
If Nv=mv, the associated solution of a differential equation obeys Y(t+P)=mY(t) at every time, not merely at the sampled times. In particular, Nv=v gives a nonzero P-periodic solution, and every nonzero P-periodic solution arises this way. If Nv=−v, the state changes sign after one period and repeats after two. A unit-modulus Floquet multiplier different from 1 need not give repetition after one period, and a generalized eigenvector in a nontrivial Jordan block need not even give bounded motion.
For the scalar example under periodic solution, N is the one-by-one matrix (e2πa). Numerically solving a matrix problem uses the same idea: integrate one initial value problem for each column of X(0)=I through one period, then compute the eigenvalues of X(P). This is useful when an explicit solution of a differential equation is unavailable: one period determines the Floquet growth rate over arbitrarily many periods.
For piecewise constant coefficients, which are also covered by the one-period construction, N is the time-ordered product of the segment matrix exponentials, with the earliest segment on the right. For example, take period P=2 and alternate
K1​=(00​10​)(0≤t<1),K2​=(01​00​)(1≤t<2).

N=eK2​eK1​=(11​12​),m±​=23±5​​,γ=21​log23+5​​≈0.4812.

Replacing the coefficient by its mean would instead give eK1​+K2​=(cosh1sinh1​sinh1cosh1​) and the incorrect rate 0.5. The matrices do not commute. The scalar mean-coefficient formula therefore cannot simply be transferred to matrix systems. Nevertheless the Liouville formula for a fundamental matrix gives the correct determinant even in the noncommuting case:

In the example, this is 1=m+​m−​; it fixes the product of the Floquet multipliers, rather than either multiplier separately.
In Sur les équations différentielles linéaires à coefficients périodiques (1883), Gaston Floquet calls a function satisfying f(t+P)=mf(t) periodic of the second kind, and distinguishes the genuinely periodic function obtained when m=1. This historical terminology captures precisely the difference between repetition of the coefficient and repetition of the state.[ref]

A homogeneous linear differential equation is a linear differential equation with identically zero forcing term, L[y]=0. On a common interval, its solutions of a differential equation form the vector space kerL, the kernel of a linear map. They include the zero function and are closed under addition and scalar multiplication. For any two solutions of a differential equation u,v and constant scalars α,β, linearity gives L[αu+βv]=α0+β0=0: this is the superposition principle. The scalars must be constant; variable multipliers introduce extra derivatives.
For example, y′+2y=0 has general solution y=Ce−2t, where C is any constant real number. A short verification uses the product rule: (e2ty)′=e2t(y′+2y)=0, so e2ty is constant. For y1​=e−2t and y2​=2e−2t, the sum is 3e−2t and also solves the same homogeneous linear differential equation. At t=1, their values are approximately 0.13534, 0.27067 and 0.40601. Every curve is a multiple of one exponential function; the solution space of a homogeneous linear differential equation has dimension one. Both t and y in this example and the following diagram are dimensionless mathematical variables.
Now keep the same differential operator L[y]=y′+2y but prescribe the forcing term 1. The inhomogeneous linear differential equation y′+2y=1 has particular solution yp​=1/2 and general solution y=1/2+Ce−2t. The initial conditions y(0)=0,1,2 select, respectively,
u0​(t)=21​(1−e−2t),u1​(t)=21​+21​e−2t,u2​(t)=21​+23​e−2t.

At t=1, their values are approximately 0.43233, 0.56767 and 0.70300. The midpoint 21​(u0​+u2​)=u1​ solves the same inhomogeneous linear differential equation, because L[21​(u0​+u2​)]=21​(1+1)=1. The sum s=u0​+u2​=1+e−2t instead satisfies s′+2s=2, so it fails the equation with forcing term 1. More generally, a linear combination of solutions of a differential equation for the same fixed nonzero forcing term retains that forcing term precisely when its scalar weights add to one. This is the affine space structure, rather than unrestricted superposition within that fixed family.
On the left, all three curves solve the same homogeneous linear differential equation. On the right, u0​,u1​,u2​ share the particular solution 1/2, and the shaded difference u2​−1/2 is the homogeneous solution 23​e−2t. The dashed sum has twice the forcing term, even though its starting value coincides with that of u2​. Adding the two initial conditions also adds their inputs; taking their midpoint averages both. This distinction makes the superposition principle useful for assembling responses to different inputs without mistaking that assembly for a solution of a differential equation with the original input. See MIT's superposition notes, including the particular solution one half.

A solution that is a continuously differentiable function up to the corner necessarily satisfies g′(b)=q(d): differentiating the top boundary trace in its tangential x direction gives ux​(b,d)=g′(b), while the right-edge condition gives the same partial derivative as q(d).

If it fails, a solution can still satisfy the interior equation and the boundary conditions on open edges while failing to have a continuous first derivative at that corner. In particular, homogeneous right-edge Neumann boundary conditions require g′(b)=0 for a solution continuously differentiable at the top-right corner. Boundary values may remain continuous even when this derivative requirement fails.

A first-exit argument proves preservation of a bound by contradiction at the earliest time the bound could fail. An estimate valid up to that contact can then rule the contact out. This is useful before a global supremum norm is known to be finite.
For example, suppose a continuous y with ∣y(0)∣<R satisfies ∣y(t)∣≤B+cmax0≤s≤t​∣y(s)∣2, where B+cR2<R. At a first time T with ∣y(T)∣=R, the estimate gives R≤B+cR2<R, a contradiction. Hence ∣y(t)∣<R for every finite time. A separate uniform estimate is needed to conclude supt≥0​∣y(t)∣<R, since pointwise strict inequalities alone allow equality of the supremum.

Ordinary differential equation OurBigBook.com
A Bernoulli differential equation is a first-order ordinary differential equation of the displayed form, with P and Q continuous functions on an interval and a fixed real exponent n. A nonlinear power can hide a first-order linear differential equation: on a suitable branch, the Bernoulli power substitution z=y1−n removes it exactly. The transformed solution of a differential equation can be completely regular even when recovering y produces finite-time blowup.
For example, the reciprocal Bernoulli equation with finite-time blowup y′+y=exy2 becomes z′−z=−ex under z=1/y. The initial conditions y(0)=1/2 and y(0)=−1 select a positive trajectory blowing up at x=2 and a negative trajectory tending to zero as x→∞, respectively. The integrating factor exposes both behaviors with the same short calculation.
The cases n=0 and n=1 are already first-order linear differential equations: respectively y′+Py=Q, with the zeroth-power term interpreted as the constant 1, and y′+(P−Q)y=0. There is no need for a nonlinear change of variable; for n=1, y1−n=1 would discard the unknown entirely. For other exponents, the substitution must respect the domain of exponentiation and may lose the zero solution of a differential equation.[ref]
